title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning
extended_summary:
This preprint examines how pre-service elementary science teachers incorporated ChatGPT into lesson planning and what they believed the tool could and could not do in science instruction. The study was motivated by a gap between optimistic claims about generative AI in education and the limited empirical evidence showing how it is actually used in classroom-oriented planning.

The intervention/context consisted of a short professional-learning experience on ChatGPT followed by an assignment in which 29 pre-service teachers at a Korean teachers' university created elementary science lesson plans that used ChatGPT. Participants also attached simulated ChatGPT conversations and completed open-ended survey questions about their reasoning, anticipated benefits, and concerns. The authors evaluated the plans with a modified TPACK-based technology-integration rubric and analyzed the survey responses qualitatively.

The pre-service teachers envisioned ChatGPT supporting a wide range of science topics and instructional approaches, especially cooperative learning, POE, the learning cycle, analogy generation, and concept mapping. Overall lesson-plan quality was moderately high, but participants were weaker at selecting the most appropriate ChatGPT functions than at aligning ChatGPT with goals and instructional strategies. They saw potential for questioning, individualized support, and formative feedback, but also worried about inaccurate or misleading outputs, hallucinated or non-existent resources, and student overreliance. The paper concludes that AI literacy, critical checking, and structured classroom interactions are necessary to mitigate these risks and that future research should test ChatGPT in real science classrooms rather than only in lesson plans.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's LLM-based conversational AI chatbot for generating and refining text, answering questions, and supporting interactive dialogue.
identified_tools.use_case: Pre-service elementary science teachers used ChatGPT in lesson-plan design for science instruction, including content expansion, role-play scripting, individualized support, formative feedback, and simulated teacher/student interactions.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative/mixed-methods study of 29 pre-service elementary science teachers, lesson plans integrating ChatGPT received an average modified TPACK-based TIAR score of M=3.29 (SD=.91) on a 4-point scale. Scores were higher for curriculum goals & ChatGPT (M=3.44, SD=.87) and instructional strategies & ChatGPT (M=3.48, SD=.99) than for ChatGPT function selection(s) (M=3.00, SD=.93); the difference between items 2 and 3 was significant, t(28)=2.3173, p=.0280.

The paper reports that some uses of ChatGPT were appropriate, such as supporting extended questioning, role-play organization, and concise summarization, but others were inappropriate or unreliable, including nonexistent YouTube links, inaccurate or non-existent materials, and use in visually oriented tasks where ChatGPT was poorly matched. The authors also note risks of overdependence, hallucination, and pedagogical misalignment in lesson planning.
findings.measure: Qualitative analysis of lesson plans and survey responses

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-methods preprint focused on lesson plans and perceptions rather than a controlled effectiveness study. It provides useful empirical evidence about how ChatGPT was planned for instructional use and about concerns such as hallucinations and overreliance, but causal evidence is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports mixed practical implications rather than outcome gains or harms on student achievement, and no effect size is provided. Its main impact is descriptive: it surfaces both promising uses and clear risks in teacher planning with ChatGPT.
